episodes.title: The Internet Might Need To Shut Down...
episodes.summary: Mutahar argues that a cluster of recent internet-security stories illustrates a worsening digital-risk environment. He focuses on what he calls “HTTP-to-shell,” describing a purported vulnerability in Google’s Brotli compression decoder that could allegedly enable memory corruption, information disclosure, denial of service, or code execution when malformed compressed data is processed. He says exposure may arise through inbound requests, automatically decoded outbound responses, or direct decompression, including URL previews, webhooks, crawlers, and image proxies. The episode then broadens to artificial intelligence: Mutahar contends that coding and reverse-engineering models are accelerating vulnerability research and exploit development, while less-restricted models make safeguards easier to bypass. He also discusses alleged device surveillance, account restrictions, and competition among AI companies. His central prediction is that security fears could motivate tighter regulation, platform consolidation, and reduced privacy or self-hosting. The source presents these points as commentary and speculation; several technical names and examples are unclear in the captions and require independent verification.
